tables.title: Table 2: The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.
notes: Residual Dropout: We apply dropout [33] to the output of each sub-layer, before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized. In addition, we apply dropout to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks. For the base model, we use a rate of P_drop = 0.1.
Label Smoothing: During training, we employed label smoothing of value ε_ls = 0.1 [36]. This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.
Footnote 5: We used values of 2.8, 3.7, 6.0 and 9.5 TFLOPS for K80, K40, M40 and P100, respectively.

observations: Table 2 compares BLEU scores (EN-DE and EN-FR) and Training Cost (FLOPS) across multiple models including ByteNet, Deep-Att + PosUnk, GNMT + RL, ConvS2S, MoE, ensembles thereof, and two Transformer variants (base and big).

The column headers for BLEU and Training Cost are duplicated with subheaders 'EN-DE' and 'EN-FR' under them, implying two columns per metric; the JSON schema reflects this by repeating column names as distinct keys.
Numerical values include scientific notation (e.g., '2.3 · 10^19'), decimal numbers (e.g., '23.75'), and some cells are empty (represented as null).
The footnote marker '5' appears in the text referencing TFLOPS values for GPU types; this is captured in notes.
uncertainties: The exact alignment of column headers in the original table is ambiguous due to formatting: 'BLEU' and 'Training Cost (FLOPS)' appear as top-level headers with subheaders 'EN-DE' and 'EN-FR'. The schema preserves the literal column strings as given, resulting in duplicate keys; this may cause ambiguity in strict JSON parsing unless handled by application logic.
Some rows have missing entries (e.g., row 6 has null for BLEU EN-DE and Training Cost EN-DE), which are preserved as null per instruction.
The phrase '3.3 · 10^18' uses a middle dot (·) and caret (^) for exponentiation; these are retained verbatim as in source.
